detail.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence changes the risk problem for financial institutions because increasingly autonomous systems can move beyond generating an answer or recommendation and carry a decision into action. They can interpret an objective, choose tools, move between systems, adapt when an expected route fails and execute at machine speed. This paper argues that, as those capabilities expand, part of the institution's risk moves into the execution path itself. It develops the Agentic Governance Triangle as a practical way to frame the resulting trade-off among Agent Autonomy, Speed and Scale, and Provable Control and Accountability. Drawing on recent supervisory guidance, emerging runtimegovernance approaches and observed agent behaviour, the paper shows why controls designed around policy, pre-deployment testing and after-the-fact assurance may not be sufficient when an agent can select its own route to an outcome. The Continuous Execution Governance Stack (CEGS) is presented as a runtime governance architecture that carries risk appetite, delegated authority, operating limits, evidence and intervention into the action boundary, the point where an AI decision is about to create an external consequence. CEGS does not remove the trade-offs represented by the triangle. Its purpose is to make them more precise and governable, allowing institutions to expand a safe operating footprint while keeping consequential actions within authority, risk appetite and regulatory expectations. The paper closes with implications for testing, board oversight and the governance of autonomous execution in financial services.

detail.abstract: Can a stablecoin's recent price behaviour tell us whether it will lose its peg within the next week? I train a gradient-boosted classifier on daily DeFiLlama data for 219 USD-pegged stablecoins (December 2020 to October 2026) to estimate the probability that a coin trading within 0.5% of $1 today will trade at least 1% away from $1 within seven days. The model is fitted on data before July 2024, calibrated on the second half of 2024, and evaluated on forecast dates from January 2025 to October 17, 2026; forecast dates whose outcome window would cross into the next period are removed before each split. On 55,702 test coin-days, it reaches an average precision (AP) of 0.59, against 0.44 for a simple rule based on the worst deviation of the past 30 days and 0.11 for random ranking. At a 20% alert threshold, it flags 76% of eligible forecast dates subsequently followed by a depeg, with 42% of alerts followed by a depeg; counted by distinct episode, 65% of the 2,224 test-period depegs were preceded by an alert in the prior seven days. The model's probabilities run high in the test period, which was calmer than the period used for calibration. The model's AP exceeds the simple rule's at every threshold and horizon tested, but the margin narrows for larger moves and is negligible for 3% moves over fourteen days. Recent volatility and the number of recent off-peg days carry most of the signal; supply features show no consistent improvement across validation and test periods. The model's skill falls steadily with coin size, and for coins with at least $1 billion in circulation it demonstrates no predictive skill in this small event sample. I describe a live forward test that began in October 2026.

detail.abstract: Organizations increasingly face the challenge of integrating advanced technologies while responding to rapid market changes, economic uncertainty, and global disruptions. Although technological capabilities continue to evolve, successful implementation often depends on organizational factors that enable adaptation and change. Among these factors, organizational culture and organizational learning have emerged as critical determinants of technology integration, yet the literature remains fragmented regarding their relationship. This qualitative study examines how organizational culture and organizational learning shape the implementation of advanced technologies through a comprehensive review of academic literature from the 1960s to the present. detail.abstract: This paper asks which combination of grid service, onsite generation, storage and cooling gives a 100–300 MW data center campus the best resilience and regulatory fit for energization before 2030. The method combines a review of grid-operator, regulator and company documents current to October 2026, engineering estimates for a 200 MW reference design, and a cost model published with the paper. The governing judgment is that electricity supply, not water, limits new capacity in Virginia and in most other markets examined; water use is set by the cooling design, and direct-to-chip liquid cooling with closed-loop dry heat rejection takes process water out of the siting question in temperate climates. The configuration designed to meet the proposed ride-through rules, ride out a winter gas event or a grid outage, and qualify as a synthetic minor air source is firm utility service, a grid-forming battery, dual-fuel reciprocating engines limited to outages and emergencies, and warm-water liquid cooling. On a common UPS and ride-through baseline, with the grid bill built from Dominion's tariff sheets, it models at $34–35/MWh, about $69 million a year, above grid-only service with diesel backup; the difference buys outage endurance and grid-forming transfer, not energy. Zoning, air permits and tariff rules, not equipment, decide what onsite generation may do. Nuclear and geothermal supply are not available to a Virginia campus this decade.

detail.abstract: The patent system plays a significant role in encouraging technological innovation, protecting intellectual property, and promoting economic development. However, complicated filing requirements, lengthy examination periods, procedural formalities, and the cost of patent prosecution may discourage inventors, startups, universities, and small enterprises from seeking patent protection. Between 2014 and 2025, India introduced several amendments to its patent rules and related legislation intended to improve administrative efficiency, simplify procedural requirements, facilitate electronic filing, and make the patent system more accessible. Important developments include the Patents (Amendment) Rules, 2016, subsequent amendments in 2019 and 2020, the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021, the Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023, and the Patents (Amendment) Rules, 2024 [1-8]. This article examines the principal patent-related amendments introduced during the period, their implications for applicants and patent administration, and the continuing challenges associated with procedural simplification. It argues that procedural reform should not be measured solely by the reduction of forms, deadlines, or penalties. Rather, effective reform requires a balanced framework that combines accessible procedures, predictable timelines, transparent decision-making, adequate examination capacity, and meaningful protection for inventors and the public.

detail.abstract: I estimate the causal effects of Berkeley, California's soda tax policy, passed in November 2014, on firms' advertising strategies and advertising elasticity in Berkeley across major diet and regular soda brands. Using weekly sales and advertising spending data from 2014 to 2015, I use a comprehensive sample of products and employ a combination of a difference-indifferences framework and a border-market identification strategy to estimate causal impacts. While existing literature provides evidence of advertising effectiveness across various products from a marketing perspective, I examine how this effectiveness changes under soda tax policies, a public health tool frequently used to mitigate the health risks of excessive sugar intake from soft drink consumption. I find evidence that the own traditional advertising elasticity, measuring the relative change in current and future demand due to changes in own traditional advertising, for regular soda declined by 0.023, falling from a pre-policy value of 0.014 to a post-policy elasticity of-0.009. This indicates that advertising became less effective in the taxed category compared to untaxed beverages. I also find evidence that firms reduced advertising spending for regular soda by approximately 16.4% overall, with declines of 16.1% and 39.2% relative to diet soda and light beer, respectively, in the post-policy Berkeley. Additionally, firms adopted spatial marketing strategies, reducing advertising spending near Berkeley while increasing it in more distant areas. These findings offer new insights into soda tax policies and have important implications for manufacturers' pricing, profitability and marketing strategies, as well as for policymakers regarding public health outcomes.

detail.abstract:
Childcare shortages have limited families’ access to quality care, with consequences for children’s development and parents’ careers. We link two decades of childcare supply data to longitudinal surveys of U.S. scientists. We find workplace childcare deserts are widespread: more than half of scientists at universities and research institutions work in deserts, where supply falls significantly short of demand. We further find mothers working in deserts are less likely to attain tenure. They are also more likely to move to industry and part-time positions. Reduced work time partly accounts for the tenure association but other reasons remain. Expanding childcare availability near workplaces may help retain scientific talent.
The US childcare system is characterized by limited access, high costs, and uneven quality. While the COVID-19 pandemic brought the childcare crisis into sharp focus (1-4), the problem is decades old (5, 6). For years, the limited availability of affordable, high-quality childcare has strained American families (7). Yet public investment in childcare remains low relative to that of other high-income countries (8, 9). Only a handful of US states provide publicly funded preschool, and such programs primarily serve 4-year-olds only (10). For younger children, public care provision is much more limited (11), leaving families largely dependent on private providers. The labor-intensive nature of childcare, regulatory requirements, and lack of economies of scale constrain providers’ ability to expand capacity. As a result, childcare shortages are widespread (12, 13). At the same time, childcare providers often struggle financially despite low wages in the sector and high costs borne by families.
Among the many challenges facing the US childcare system, limited availability is particularly consequential because families cannot use care that is simply unavailable. Before the pandemic, 73% of center-based childcare providers reported turning families away because they were full or maintaining a waiting list in 2019 (14). More recent national data also show persistent access difficulties (15). Limited access to childcare can reduce labor-force participation (9, 16, 17). Moreover, because responsibility for the care of young children continues to fall disproportionately on women (18, 19), childcare shortages may also contribute to gender disparities in education and career advancement. These constraints can be especially consequential in scientific careers. A growing literature documents associations between parenthood and researchers’ career trajectories and outcomes (20-23), yet much less is known about how the environments in which scientists work can support—or constrain—parents’ careers. Although parental leave can provide important support around childbirth (9), the demands of caregiving extend far beyond the first months of a child’s life. Because broadly available public education generally does not begin until kindergarten, families remain heavily dependent on childcare throughout children’s early years. In the absence of reliable care, researchers may leave or change professions, reduce their work activities, or reconsider family formation.

detail.abstract: With electricity being a commodity of substantial economic and social impact, the efficiency of its forward trading is tightly scrutinized by regulators. In particular, the forward premium between the liquid day ahead auctions and the real time delivery prices has been a major focus of attention for risk and conduct. The typical day-ahead uniform price auction essentially takes limit orders, ie offers from generators to produce at any price at or above their offer price, and vice-versa for retailer bids to consume. Whilst the no-arbitrage zero forward premium is often taken to indicate efficiency, we show this is not sufficient. We analyse this by considering limit order pair trading. A limit order pair is a simultaneous offer and bid at a particular value into the day ahead market such that if the clearing price is above that value, the sell is activated, and if it is below, the buy is activated. We derive optimal conditions and show that even if the forward premium is zero, this strategy may be profitable; also confirmed by empirical analysis from GB and Japan, two markets that differ vastly in their maturities. We discuss the robustness of this market analysis and its significance for the persistence of forward premia. In particular, and surprisingly, we show that forward premia can be sustained from a new risk neutral perspective alongside the existing risk-aversion and market power explanations. More generally, this suggests a broader consideration of market efficiency in an actively traded physical commodity such as electricity.

detail.abstract: Blockchains are not currencies. They are public records that no one owns and someone must keep, and the rules that decide who pays for that keeping, who is paid, and for what are each network’s fiscal constitution. Bitcoin’s founding design paid strangers to support the network, and the Ethereum white paper chose perpetual issuance expressly to reduce wealth concentration and give future generations “a fair chance to acquire currency units.” Ethereum then took a different turn. Under the banner of “ultrasound money,” it came to tax its users, burn the proceeds as a dividend to holders, and pay its security budget as a yield on capital. The result is a centripetal network: by mid-2026, four entities accounted for just over half of staked ether, three of them regulated corporations. This Article argues that the turn was a strategic error. An ecosystem that makes useful work broadly accessible can acquire what no cryptography can supply: a constituency, provided its earners would lose something real if the common infrastructure were closed and can act independently of the applications that pay them. Drawing on policy-feedback theory, the Article explains why paid constituencies make institutions costly to repeal, from Civil War pensions to the Alaska dividend, and where that protection erodes. Drawing on securities law, it argues that rewards for independently supplied services stand on different ground from a promoter’s promise of profit, though work is no exemption and the tokens paid may still be securities. Drawing on comparative constitutional law, it examines how proportionality review can protect the freedom to trade against crypto restrictions. The Article then shows national governments and private fortunes building paid constituencies of their own, and locates Ethereum’s opportunity in a global earning economy that no single patron controls. It proposes a program for a centrifugal Ethereum and asks how, in the age of superintelligence, machine demand could finance human livelihoods. The ambition is a billion earners. The test is whether they have an open network worth defending. Support the network, and the network supports you. That was the founding bargain. It is also the only one that scales.

detail.abstract: In this work, we developed Quantx, an exchangestyle paper-trading workspace for National Stock Exchange of India (NSE) equities in which simulated orders are matched locally against streamed market depth and protected by transactional state snapshots. The system is organized as four tiers: a React client, a FastAPI service tier, an in-process market-data decoding and matching tier, and a PostgreSQL ledger paired with a Redis quote cache. Its foundational design principle is a strict architectural boundary between a marketdata plane, which may only read authentication, instrument, and quote data from upstream providers, and an accounting plane, which alone creates orders, fills, statutory charges, cash movements, positions, and recovery snapshots; paper orders are never routed to an external broker or exchange order interface. Inside this boundary, the system normalizes prices to tick size, validates circuit, board-lot, and freeze constraints, walks five-level bid and ask depth with partial fills, applies product-aware brokerage and Indian statutory charges, discards duplicate and older-timestamp packets, refuses market orders when depth is stale, and provides atomic SafePoint state rollback alongside non-destructive multi-modal What-If stress testing and a guardrailed non-advisory learning guide. We evaluated the integrated workflow against a last-price, zerocharge, arrival-order baseline (B0) across N = 50 scripted orders spanning Typical (N1 = 20), Boundary (N2 = 20), and Adversarial (N3 = 10 valid orders plus N adv = 50 injected fault events) scenario profiles on a live PostgreSQL 16.15 and Redis 7.4.11 stack. Quantx achieved zero ledgerreconciliation error (mean = 0.00 IN R, max = 0.00 IN R vs. B0 mean = 19,684.41 IN R, max = 227,398.32 IN R), zero fill-price deviation (0.00 IN R/share vs. B0 1.60 IN R/share across N f = 73 fills), zero charge deviation (0.00 IN R/f ill vs. B0 33.08 IN R/f ill), and zero adversarial fault leaks across all 50 injected disorder, staleness, idempotency, and ruleviolation events, while maintaining sub-millisecond quote ingestion (p99 = 0.06 ms) and sub-120 ms five-level match-andcommit latency (p50 = 71.02 ms, p99 = 118.02 ms). These results support the engineering feasibility of boundary-enforced local paper execution for NSE equity practice; they do not establish fidelity to live exchange queue priority, educational learning outcomes, or production brokerage readiness.

detail.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence into organizational decision-making has been predominantly theorized through frameworks of augmentation, automation, or substitution which presuppose a clear ontological boundary between human and machine cognition. Drawing on theories of distributed cognition, sociomateriality, and the extended mind, this article argues that this boundary is increasingly untenable and develops the concept of cognitive entanglement as a condition in which human and artificial intelligence become so deeply co-constitutive in organizational decision processes that their individual contributions cannot be meaningfully decomposed. The research theorizes three stages through which organizations progress toward cognitive entanglement: complementarity, co-adaptation, and inseparability. Each stage articulates how foundational assumptions of management theory such as bounded rationality, identifiable agency, and attributable accountability are progressively destabilized. The research develops a set of formal propositions linking technological, organizational, and institutional antecedents to the depth of cognitive entanglement, and examines its consequences for strategic decision quality, organizational legitimacy, corporate governance, and international strategy. The framework contributes to emerging debates on algorithmic organizations, the micro-foundations of AI-driven strategy, and the philosophical underpinnings of management theory in an era of pervasive machine intelligence.

detail.abstract: In this work, we developed DhanSathi, an offlinefirst Android application and asynchronous backend decisionsupport system designed to provide smallholder farmers with multilingual crop advisories, seasonal financial parsing, and government scheme discovery. The evaluated workflow couples a local Room (SQLite) database and Firebase cloud synchronization engine on the mobile client with an asynchronous FastAPI backend powered by Llama 3.3 (70B) inference via the Groq LPU API. To prevent arithmetic and regulatory hallucinations in agricultural welfare matching, the system separates natural language processing from eligibility computation: deterministic backend lookup tables verify farmer eligibility rules across central and state schemes, while the language model is restricted to structured intent extraction, conversational summarization, and regional language translation (English, Hindi, and Marathi) enforced via strict Pydantic schema validation and retry handling. Offline data modifications are reconciled upon reconnection using a deterministic timestamp-based Last-Write-Wins (LWW) conflict resolution protocol. We evaluate the proof-of-concept across synthetic farmer profiles, multilingual financial ledger inputs, and government scheme corpora, measuring end-to-end inference latency, Pydantic schema validity rates, and offlineto-cloud synchronization convergence. These results support the feasibility of combining offline-first mobile persistence, schemaconstrained LLM parsing, and deterministic rule verification for low-connectivity agricultural workflows; they do not establish certified agronomic diagnosis or autonomous financial auditing.

detail.abstract: We study a multidimensional mechanism design problem where a seller offers multiple products to a single buyer. The seller possesses only marginal distributional information about the buyer's random valuation of each product. The buyer is not a perfect optimizer and satisfices whenever his utility is ϵ away from the optimum---a notion called approximate incentive compatibility (IC). We establish that the optimal separable mechanism first allocates the tolerance ϵ among the products and then screens each product separately under approximate IC. Although separable mechanisms may not be optimal for approximate IC, we provide an error bound on the separation gap. As a byproduct of bounding the separation gap, we also establish that strong duality holds for the stochastic multidimensional mechanism design problem under both approximate and exact IC. To compute the optimal mechanism, we first propose a discrete approximation that can be reformulated as a scalable finite-dimensional convex program; we then devise an oracle that efficiently extends solutions to the discretized problem into feasible mechanisms on the full valuation space with strong performance guarantees. Together with the separation gap, this shows that the solution from our discretized problem provides a provable guarantee while remaining computationally tractable.

detail.abstract: A conviction establishes liability to punishment. It does not, by itself, explain why that punishment must take place in prison. This legal and policy analysis proposes a limited federal pilot requiring a funded, verified community sentencing plan for eligible defendants and explicit reasons when imprisonment is chosen. A community sentence would impose enforceable restrictions tailored to the offense, with necessary support available regardless of income. The proposal builds on existing duties to explain sentences by requiring a concrete alternative and a reviewable comparison. A separate, expressly authorized track would examine continued custody for eligible prison-camp residents. A targeted review of published research and official reports identifies grounds for testing alternatives, contrary findings favoring imprisonment in some settings, and documented barriers to timely community placement. Published sentencing and cost figures establish context rather than a count of eligible camp residents or a savings estimate. The framework specifies eligibility, victim participation, evidentiary procedures, proportionate responses to violations and independent evaluation. Safety, victim repayment, family responsibilities and public expenditure would be measured rather than assumed to improve. Congress should fund a limited pilot, require publication of reasons and outcomes, and condition expansion on the results. Camp capacity would decline only as the need for confinement declines.

detail.abstract: Federated fine-tuning is frequently proposed as a way to adapt large language models (LLMs) across institutions without pooling their confidential corpora. Yet retaining source records locally does not, by itself, prevent disclosure through model updates, aggregate parameters, metadata or generated outputs. This critical narrative review examines how parameter-efficient adaptation, aggregation protocols, differential privacy and cryptographic protections interact with these distinct exposure channels. It draws on foundational and recent literature on federated optimisation, low-rank adaptation, inference attacks, privacy mechanisms and governance. The analysis distinguishes communication efficiency from privacy guarantees, explains why averaging low-rank factors is not generally equivalent to averaging their products, and identifies tensions between hiding client updates and detecting malicious contributions. Building on these findings, the paper articulates an assurance-oriented conceptual framework comprising seven operational layers linked by a versioned evidence record. The framework is intended to make protected units, adversary assumptions, training configuration, evaluation outcomes and deployment approvals auditable across changes. It is a design proposal, not a validated security mechanism: no original experiments, quantitative performance results or privacy guarantees are reported. A prospective evaluation agenda is presented for comparing utility, leakage, robustness, fairness and operational cost. The central conclusion is that responsible federated LLM adaptation requires a documented combination of technical controls and institutional decision-making rather than reliance on data locality or small parameter updates alone.

detail.abstract:
For more than a century, newspapers were among the most profitable businesses in media, sustained by a profit-center model built on display advertising, classified advertising, and subscription and copy sales. This paper argues that the collapse of that model over the past twenty-five years was caused not by a failure of journalism but by a failure of the container that tried to replace paper. After 1995, newspapers started moving into the web browser — a scroll-based environment designed for weak 1990s hardware. The browser eliminated the four structural pillars of newspaper economics — scarcity, hierarchy, adjacency, and completeness — replacing fixed pages, bound issues, and premium positions with loose pages anchored only at the top-left, a two-sided geometry that cannot behave like a publication. In abandoning the complete, bound issue — the dated commercial unit that defined all periodicals — newspapers lost the product that made their economics work. Global print revenues fell sharply, and as income declined, the immovable costs of print and distribution became increasingly unsustainable, driving thousands of titles to closure.

The paper contends that the browser era was a thirty-year profit center aberration that is now ending. Smart glasses and spatial computing — the biggest device race since the smartphone, with more than fifty companies worldwide developing hardware — introduce a coming reading environment of anchored surfaces, bounded pages, and page-turn navigation in which publications can once again behave like physical newspapers. The paper sets out the requirements for a new, fully three-dimensional, GPU-accelerated publishing container: print-quality internal typography, fast navigation and linking, native spatial interactivity, built-in copyright protection, and integrated analytics that measure true dwell time from two simple signals: which page is being read and when the reader turned to it.

This four-sided 3D digital paper in a bound 3D publication restores the economic logic of print while removing its largest and least flexible cost: print and distribution. The paper shows how each revenue line revives — display advertising through a restored rate card, real readers, and fixed premium positions; classified advertising through professionally focused vertical titles; and subscription and copy sales through the Kindle model of complete issues that readers own. Because content ecosystems form before hardware matures, publishers should begin building for spatial computing now. The paper concludes that the newspaper is not obsolete — it was trapped in the wrong economic model when forced to compete with web advertising — and that a new optimistic golden age of publishing is within reach.

The collapse of print economics was caused by the browser’s geometry, not by journalism. By restoring the fixed page and bound issue in 3D, this paper shows how the profit-center model returns — display, classifieds, subscriptions, and copy sales — with the potential to be stronger than at any point in the print era.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the structural impacts of the rise of the attention economy on macroeconomic growth and wealth distribution in contemporary capitalism. Building upon Thomas Piketty's thesis on patrimonial capitalism and the dominance of the rate of return on capital over the economic growth rate, alongside Mariana Mazzucato's deconstruction of value extraction versus value creation mechanisms, this study introduces the concept of "algorithmic rent" as a third channel for deepening economic inequality and draining the productive base. The paper develops a theoretical talent-allocation model grounded in classical endogenous growth literature, demonstrating how the highly skewed distribution of returns on social media platforms, coupled with cognitive survivorship bias and zero marginal publishing costs, distorts the incentive structure for young human capital. The study mathematically proves that the exodus of talent from R&D and physical production sectors toward attention-extraction activities, in parallel with the recycling of advertising surpluses into real estate and financial asset markets, generates a dual shock that depresses total factor productivity growth while elevating the rentier return on assets, thereby exacerbating the structural gap between capital returns and labor returns.

detail.abstract: Digital communication and collaboration technologies enabled remote work to expand at an unprecedented scale during the COVID-19 pandemic. Whereas prior research has examined how remote work affects the workers and firms that adopt it, less is known about its consequences for local businesses that cannot adopt it because their services require physical co-presence. This study examines how the pandemic-induced shift toward remote work reshaped economic activity within U.S. metropolitan areas. Using county-level GDP by industry from 2015 to 2024, we first show that the retail and hospitality sectors in central counties declined relative to peripheral counties after 2020, while total GDP shows no clear difference. We then use a Bartik shift-share design that instruments MSA-level work-from-home adoption with pre-pandemic industry teleworkability. The estimates indicate that a 10 percentage-point larger increase in remote-work adoption lowered GDP in these two sectors in central counties by about 10 percent, with no statistically significant effect on total GDP or on other industries. These results suggest that digitally enabled remote work generates spillovers beyond adopting organizations: by changing where people work, digital technologies change where people spend, reducing the demand for consumer-oriented services.

detail.abstract: The United States does not learn that a new disease is spreading until weeks or months after the first infection. This paper measures that delay, explains why it matters for defense against biological weapons, and proposes what Congress can do. In seven outbreaks of new or newly arrived pathogens since 2002, the time from the start of spread, as estimated or first observed, to recognition ran from about seven weeks to two years, with a median of about thirteen weeks. Establishing who or what caused an outbreak takes longer: three documented deliberate or concealed biological events took from just over one year to thirteen years to resolve. The 2026 Annual Threat Assessment reports that states with weapons programs are developing capabilities designed to defeat detection and attribution. In 2025 and 2026 the federal offices charged with integration and attribution were dismantled, emptied or left unsettled. The paper sets out three changes in law and the measure that would test each: one accountable official who publishes three response intervals every year; permanent authority and funding for wastewater surveillance and pathogen-agnostic sequencing; and a standing attribution protocol with legal limits on the use of health data. No published evidence shows how many days these changes would save. The reporting requirement is how Congress would find out.

detail.abstract: Security Champions programmes tend to follow the same arc. In the first year, the numbers look good: champions are recruited, coverage is reached, awareness scores rise, and the champions form a lively community. In the second year, awareness numbers stay high, behaviour numbers stay flat, and more effort doesn't move them. Existing maturity models cannot explain this arc because they grade programmes by activity and governance rather than by what the programme's network can carry. In this paper, I propose a maturity model for Security Champions programmes whose stages are defined by carrying capacity: how much social reinforcement a behaviour can require and still spread through the network from the champions. Drawing on the distinction between simple contagion, which spreads through single exposures, and complex contagion, which requires reinforcement from multiple contacts, I argue that the familiar arc is structural. Early stages of a programme build a network that carries simple contagion, awareness; later stages require a differently shaped network to carry complex contagion, behaviour; and the transition between them is a wall that effort alone cannot climb. The model has five stages (Roster, Community, Embedded, Bridged and Self-sustaining) with non-compensatory gates across five dimensions. A simulation of 1,200 employees and 60 champions illustrates the wall directly: networks at the first two stages carry behaviours that need one or two reinforcing contacts, while networks at the third and fourth stages carry a behaviour that needs three contacts to reach 73 and 95 per cent of the organisation. The champion community that defines the second stage adds nothing to what reaches colleagues. I close with the measures that locate a programme on the model and the field study that would test it.

detail.abstract: A 100–300 MW data center campus should be designed on the assumption that a state intelligence service will at some point hold valid administrator credentials inside its management networks. This paper assembles the public record behind that assumption and works out what follows for architecture, technology, assurance and cost. The documented entry methods since 2021 are few and they repeat: internet-facing routers, firewalls and VPN gateways; identity keys and tokens with broad scope and long life; appliances that cannot run endpoint detection; and suppliers who hold access to their customers. Dwell times are measured in years rather than days, and exploitation on average precedes the patch, so patching cannot be the main control for an exposed system. The facility systems are weak and now matter to the grid, while no cyber rule reaches the facility as a data center: the July 2026 FERC order, the NERC alerts and the three computational-load standards that passed final ballot in October 2026 contain no cyber security requirement beyond a secure-transfer method. Confidential computing does not remove the operator from the trust boundary; five published attacks between December 2024 and September 2026 defeated AMD and Intel protections with brief physical access and inexpensive hardware. Because a defense cannot depend on knowing the technique, the paper derives eight design principles that limit consequence instead, sets out a recommended configuration and implementation sequence, and models the cyber and control-system program of a stand-alone 200 MW campus at 28–29 security staff and $9–14 million a year.

detail.abstract: Gains from trade generate prosperity, yet interpersonal exchange can falter along racial lines. We study incentivized experimental economies where participants must spontaneously initiate and sustain trading relationships with others whose race is visible. When the highest gains from trade require cross-race exchange, diverse economies underperform: welfare and specialization suffer as many retreat to autarky. This underperformance reflects not segregation into racial trading blocs, but a collapse in exchange. Opportunities for contact alone do not close the performance gap, which persists and even widens over time. To understand why, we turn to communication itself. Lower welfare is associated with less communication, fewer expressions of affiliation and achievement, and less explicit signaling of needs, deficits, and surpluses. We call this communicative misalignment: differences in shared-language use that raise search, bargaining, and coordination costs. A brief linguistic intervention equips participants with a communicative toolkit. It increases communication volume and the frequency of motivational and state-signaling language. Crucially, when gains depend on cross-race exchange, the intervention restores specialization and cross-race trade, closing the performance gap. Its effects are minimal when efficient trade need not cross race, indicating specificity rather than generic skill training. Language thus operates bidirectionally, both revealing the state of cooperation and causally shaping it. Although we examine racial boundaries, the mechanism may operate along other fault lines where interactional norms diverge, including hierarchy, geography, or culture. Language, a primary conduit of culture, can impede exchange when misaligned and facilitate it when aligned. This suggests a scalable micro-governance tool for reducing transaction costs. trade | language | race/ethnicity | segregation Significance Racially diverse communities can generate gains from specialization and trade, yet these gains often go unrealized. In experimental economies that mirror everyday exchange, participants struggle when the highest returns require cross-race trade. The shortfall reflects not segregation (sorting into same-race trading blocs) but stagnation: participants retreat from interaction and produce for themselves. We design a brief intervention encouraging motivational language and explicit signaling of needs and surpluses. By shifting how participants talk, it changes their trading behavior, increasing cross-race exchange and, consequently, welfare. Crucially, the intervention operates only where diversity impedes gains, confirming that it targets the barrier itself. These results suggest that language, not only preferences or sorting, can introduce transaction costsor reduce them.

detail.abstract: This paper examines why Kenya's trade policy architecture, though dense with tariffs, safeguards and continental commitments, treats competition as an afterthought. It argues that trade instruments allocate rents before any competition authority acts, so market structure is settled upstream of enforcement. Three episodes test the claim: twenty-four years of sugar safeguards, government-to-government fuel imports and American market access. It proposes a competition-embedded model built on three tests of origin, duration and contestability, and six institutional reforms. It concludes that embedding competition is a condition of productive trade policy, not a constraint upon it.

detail.abstract: This research systematically examines the impact of digital retail media advertising, social media marketing, and Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) on consumer engagement, brand loyalty, and purchasing decisions within the retail sector. Using a systematic literature review under the PRISMA framework, 25 peer-reviewed articles were thematically analyzed to distill the trends and gaps. Findings show that personalized digital retail advertising enhances customer conversion, while social media fosters brand loyalty through network dynamics and peer influence. However, challenges like privacy concerns, ad fatigue, and GenAI's lack of emotional authenticity were also evident. The study contributes to theoretical models such as the Hierarchy of Effects, Network Theory, and the Technology Acceptance Model by suggesting necessary updates for the digital era. Practical recommendations for retailers include investing in data-driven personalization, maintaining ethical transparency, and balancing automation with human interaction. This research underscores the increasing necessity for ethical marketing practices in a rapidly transforming digital landscape and offers insights for future academic exploration and strategic business development focused on sustaining consumer trust and engagement.

detail.abstract: This article explores equilibrium forms of proactive-positive significance and presents specific lines of reasoning and methods. It first categorizes game equilibria into Proactive-Positive Form (Jījí Xíngtài) and Passive-Negative Form (Xiāojí Xíngtài), and points out that Passive-Negative Equilibrium (Xiāojí Jūnhéng) is not conducive to realizing the maximization of overall interests, and does not constitute an equilibrium in the true sense. Traditional equilibrium concepts such as the Nash equilibrium draw no such distinction, and treat both uniformly as equilibrium states for research. The paper then puts forward Proactive-Positive Equilibrium (Jījí Jūnhéng)-characterized by unified goals, the tendency toward maximizing both individual and overall interests, proactivity, stability, objectivity, and fairness-clarifying the forms, characteristics, fundamental requirements and procedures of Proactive-Positive Equilibrium, as well as the primary steps of mechanism design for Proactive-Positive Equilibrium, illustrated with cases including "Perfect Boxed Pig Game," "Car Owner's Dilemma," and "Designed Prisoner's Dilemma." In its recommendations, the paper concludes that Proactive-Positive Equilibrium is a Stability Requirement (Wěndìng Yāoqiú) for social development, represents a long-term irreversible trend, and serves as the cornerstone for the advanced development of productivity.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether Kenya's competition regime, built for the liberalisation era, can serve a development agenda it was never calibrated to carry. Enforcement data from the 2024/25 financial year and the OECD's 2026 peer review expose a regime that settles rather than deters, regulates supplier relationships more than cartels, and relies on seven merger staff. Buyer power rules, South African public interest practice, overlapping regional merger regimes and the 2026 digital markets Bill are tested against that record. The paper proposes calibrated developmental antitrust: capacity-tiered enforcement, a public interest ledger with sunset clauses, relational power doctrine and regional subsidiarity.

detail.abstract: This paper interrogates whether competition law can discipline Kenya's downstream petroleum sector when price, supply and entry are each shaped by the state. Using regulator statistics for 2019 to 2026, it computes Herfindahl-Hirschman indices at aggregate and product level, and tests them against regulated pricing, the shift from open tendering to government-to-government importation, entry barriers and overlapping regulators. It advances an hourglass thesis: rivalry persists among 154 licensed oil marketing companies while concentration migrates to a state-coordinated import neck that conventional indices cannot see. The paper proposes upstream-aware metrics, a statutory basis for sovereign supply, and a binding concurrency protocol.

detail.abstract: Megaproject governance has become increasingly information-rich. Integrated schedules, cost systems, risk registers, dashboards, digital platforms and predictive analytics can reveal deviations with unprecedented speed and granularity. Yet improved visibility does not automatically increase the capacity to alter project outcomes. This paper introduces the concept of the control gap: the distance between the conditions a governance system can observe and the conditions it can materially influence within the time available for effective intervention. The paper develops the construct through a conceptual synthesis of megaproject governance, organizational control, information-processing, cybernetics, sensemaking and dynamic-capabilities research. It argues that control gaps emerge from four separations: visibility without authority, authority without capability, capability without timely mobilization, and intervention without reliable feedback. These separations are intensified by institutional fragmentation, contractual lock-in, external dependencies, decision latency and the progressive irreversibility of commitments. The paper distinguishes data visibility, interpretive visibility and actionability, and proposes a multi-dimensional framework for diagnosing control gaps across technical, commercial, institutional and temporal domains. It further advances six propositions concerning the relationship between visibility, influence, latency, reversibility and governance performance. The central implication is that megaproject governance should not be evaluated primarily by reporting sophistication or data volume. Its more consequential test is whether relevant signals can be interpreted, escalated and converted into proportionate action before adverse conditions become embedded in cost, schedule, contractual or political structures. The paper concludes by outlining practical mechanisms for reducing the control gap, including assumption governance, explicit decision-rights architecture, intervention windows, influence mapping, adaptive baselines and outcome-based feedback loops.
